source.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Black-Box Prompt Optimization as the Scale of LLMs Continues to Grow
source.authors: Ziyu Zhou; Yihang Wu; Jingyuan Yang; Zhan Xiao; Rongjun Li

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; Figure 1 is referenced but its plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reads in full and reports how black-box prompt-optimization gains vary with model size. It does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, architecture effects, or the listed downstream-predictability claim.
record.gate_note: The paper compares initial and optimized prompts on downstream tasks, and reports that prompt-optimization gains diminish with model size. These are findings about the efficacy of prompt optimization, not measurements of the scaling-law behaviors named by V1–V7. The paper also cites scaling-related work, but does not test those cited claims.
record.test_reason: The study measures how much black-box prompt optimization (EvoPrompt, ProTeGi, BPO) raises downstream task scores, and how that gain shrinks with model size. The authors call this an 'inverse scaling law'. The measured quantity is the gain from prompt optimization, not loss, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss. It does not cite or test the original scaling-law papers, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that black-box prompt optimization gives only limited gains on large LLMs, and that gains shrink as model size grows across Qwen-2.5 7B–72B and up to DeepSeek-V3. They attribute this to larger models' better alignment and domain understanding, which makes lexical refinements and domain cues redundant. They call their experiments preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law recipe is tested; the study evaluates black-box prompt-optimization methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported prompt-optimization gains vary with model size, dataset, and optimization method.

fits_no_version.finding: EvoPrompt's SST-5 accuracy gain falls from 12% (Qwen-2.5 7B) to 5.9% (72B) to 1.1% (DeepSeek-V3 671B). The authors say other datasets follow comparable trends.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from black-box prompt optimization diminish as LLM size increases.

fits_no_version.finding: On DeepSeek V3 and Gemini 2.0 Flash, the three optimizers give average gains of roughly 1–2%, and some method/dataset pairs decline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Black-box prompt optimization yields only marginal task-score gains on very large LLMs.

record.problems: The authors describe the experiments as preliminary. Their scale comparison uses Qwen-2.5 models up to 72B and DeepSeek-V3 at 671B, leaving intermediate sizes untested; the benchmarks are English-language and text-only. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 gives performance-improvement results across Qwen-2.5 scales and datasets, but the plotted numeric values are not present in the supplied text. The text’s explicitly stated SST-5 values are recorded in r25–r27; other figure-only values are not transcribed.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from small-run fits.
Effect of depth, width or architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of scale or loss. Only prompt-optimization gains across sizes are reported, with no fit.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'inverse scaling law' is used loosely and is not a fitted power law, so it does not bear on V1–V7. There is an internal inconsistency in the averages: the Introduction and Table 1 agree, while Section 3.3 swaps two values. Figure 1 values for 14B and 32B are not in the text. Section 4 compares model families (Qwen vs DeepSeek), which confounds size.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute.
Whether power-law fits on small runs predict loss on larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; the paper reports changes in prompt-optimization gains, not that relationship.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.
